Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.

summaries.gardner: Home Depot is a top-dog brand in its industry but fails most Rule Breaker traits: home improvement is a mature market growing a few percent a year, and the stock is down about 22% over 52 weeks rather than showing relative strength. It is a classic 'Rule Maker' incumbent, not a Rule Breaker.
summaries.buffett: Home Depot fits many Buffett tenets: a simple, understandable business with a durable scale advantage, a long profit record and about 20% returns on capital. Weaknesses are heavier debt (about $52.9B) after the SRS and GMS deals, falling margins since FY2022, and a price of about 20x trailing earnings that is fair rather than cheap.
summaries.munger: Munger would like the dominant, scale-based franchise and the strong customer-first culture inherited from the founders. He would be wary that returns are increasingly supported by leverage (equity of only $16.6B) and that the business is tied to the housing cycle, but at about 19x forward earnings it is a quality business at a fair-to-full price.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would classify Home Depot as a stalwart (and partly a cyclical tied to housing turnover) with an easy-to-understand story. With earnings growth guided at flat to 4% and a P/E near 20, the PEG is well above 1, so it is not a Lynch bargain unless one bets on a housing recovery.
summaries.fisher: Home Depot scores well on Fisher's points for sales organization, cost control, management depth and labor relations, and it keeps adding new revenue sources (SRS, GMS, Pro trade credit, AI tools). It does not do classic R&D, and recent margin declines and slow growth fall short of Fisher's demand for sustained above-average growth.
summaries.graham: Home Depot meets Graham's size, long profit record, dividend history and ten-year EPS growth tests, but fails his valuation tests badly: a P/E around 20.7 and a price-to-book near 17.8 give a product of about 367, far above 22.5, and its current ratio of about 1.08 is below Graham's preferred 2.
summaries.thiel: Home Depot is a scale incumbent, not a Zero to One company: it has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals and Lowe's offers a close substitute. It does score on distribution and durability, with a huge store and delivery network that new entrants find hard to copy.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner's approach favors companies riding big secular shifts with accelerating growth, operating discipline and a reasonable valuation. Home Depot shows discipline and cash generation but low single-digit growth, no AI-driven platform shift and a stock in a downtrend, so it fits poorly.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller focuses on liquidity, rates and earnings momentum; with 30-year mortgage rates above 7% and earnings guided only flat to up 4%, the macro backdrop works against Home Depot today. The setup could change quickly if rates fall and housing turnover recovers, which would be his catalyst.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith looks for high returns on capital, high gross margins, cash conversion and resilience; Home Depot has about 20% ROIC and strong cash generation but only a 33% gross margin and cyclical exposure to housing. At about a 5.1% free-cash-flow yield it is not overpriced, making it a reasonable but not ideal Fundsmith-type holding.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, Home Depot has a good return on capital (about 20% ROIC) but an earnings yield (EBIT/EV) of only about 5.9%, which is modest. It would rank in the middle rather than near the top of a Magic Formula screen.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool asks for an extraordinary business, talented and honest managers, and the ability to reinvest at high rates. Home Depot has the first two in good measure, but reinvestment opportunities at high returns are limited, with growth now coming mainly from acquisitions such as SRS and GMS.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai seeks simple businesses in temporary distress bought at a large discount with low downside. Home Depot is simple and its housing slump looks temporary, but at about 19x forward earnings the price does not offer the heavy discount the Dhandho approach requires.
summaries.wood: Home Depot is not a disruptive-innovation company in ARK's platforms (AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain, multiomics); it is a user of AI tools rather than a builder of them. It fits Cathie Wood's framework very poorly.
summaries.ackman: Ackman's criteria (simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative, dominant, with high barriers to entry and a strong balance sheet) fit Home Depot well, and Pershing Square has owned similar businesses. The main drawbacks are leverage and cyclicality, and the stock's 22% decline could interest a value-minded quality investor.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep favored 'scale economics shared' businesses that pass savings to customers. Home Depot uses its scale to keep prices competitive and invest in service, but it has not followed an aggressive cost-sharing model like Costco or Amazon, so it fits only partly.
summaries.valentine: Don Valentine looked for huge, fast-growing markets created by technology shifts. Home Depot serves a very large but mature market and is not riding a technological discontinuity, so it does not fit his venture-style lens.
summaries.nash: Home Depot fails most of Tom Nash's hard filters: revenue growth is far below 10%, debt far exceeds cash, operating margin is below 20%, and the stock has lagged the S&P 500 over five years. It scores about 50 of 130 on his 13-category scorecard, well short of the 75 bar.

momentum.evidence: The stock fell about 22% over the past 52 weeks to $293.92 (Oct 13, 2026) and was down about 17% year-to-date, well behind the market.

g4.evidence: It has a seasoned management bench (CEO Ted Decker, CFO Richard McPhail, Ann-Marie Campbell) and about 76% institutional ownership, but no notable famous-investor champion and the CEO is on medical leave.

g6.evidence: Some commentators call it expensive at about 19-20x earnings for low single-digit growth, but most of the 36 covering analysts rate it Buy with a $380 average target.

simple.evidence: Selling tools and building materials through 2,359 stores and to contractors via SRS is an easy business for a generalist to understand.

b2.evidence: Home Depot has been profitable every year for decades, with diluted EPS rising from about $5.46 in FY2015 to $14.23 in FY2025.

integrity.evidence: Management is candid (e.g., the CFO saying in Sept 2026 there was no sign of a demand turnaround) and the board is well governed, but the CEO also holds the chair role and insider ownership is only about 0.06%.

b6.evidence: The $18.25B SRS and $5.5B GMS acquisitions expand logically into Pro distribution, but they also mark a shift to large-scale acquisitions as Lowe's made similar Pro deals.

roic.evidence: Return on invested capital is about 20%, high and consistent, but return on equity above 100% reflects heavy use of debt (total debt about $52.9B vs equity of $16.6B).

fcf.evidence: FY2025 free cash flow was $12.6B ($16.3B operating cash flow less $3.7B capex) on $14.2B of net earnings, and trailing-twelve-month FCF was about $15.1B.

b10.evidence: Home Depot pays out most of its profit (dividends of $9.2B in FY2025); retained capital went into SRS and GMS acquisitions, yet the share price is roughly where it was five years ago.

safety.evidence: At about $294 the stock trades near 19x forward earnings and about 17.8x book value; a conservative DCF using recent ~1.6% growth and ~9.9% FCF margins gives roughly $141 per share at a 12% discount rate.

fairprice.evidence: At about 19x forward earnings and a 5.1% free-cash-flow yield, the price is reasonable for a high-quality market leader, though growth is only low single digits.

mu5.evidence: There are few ways a 2,359-store category leader with $16B of annual operating cash flow and housing-repair demand could permanently fail; the main risks are leverage and a prolonged housing slump.

reinvest.evidence: It plans about 80 new stores and Pro/SRS branch growth, but capex is only about 2.5% of sales and most cash goes to dividends, so high-return reinvestment opportunities are limited.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear stalwart/cyclical: a dominant home improvement retailer whose growth tracks housing turnover and remodeling, with an upside story if mortgage rates fall.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E is about 20.7 while FY2026 EPS is guided to grow only flat to 4%, so the P/E is far above the growth rate (PEG about 2.2).

runway.evidence: Growth can continue via the Pro market, SRS/GMS branches and about 80 planned stores within a ~$1.1 trillion addressable market, but at mid-single-digit rates, not substantial expansion.

ly7.evidence: There is no notable open-market insider buying, and buybacks have been paused since the SRS deal (no repurchases in FY2025), with diluted shares edging up from 993M to 996M.

ly8.evidence: It is a $295B Dow component covered by about 36 analysts, the opposite of overlooked.

fi2.evidence: Management keeps adding new offerings such as Pro trade credit, SRS/GMS specialty distribution, installation services and AI tools like Magic Apron, though core products are commodities it does not develop.

fi3.evidence: Home Depot does not report R&D spending; its technology investments (interconnected retail, AI tools) are not disclosed as R&D with measurable returns.

fi4.evidence: Its merchandising, Pro sales force and interconnected retail are industry-leading, generating $164.7B of sales, nearly twice Lowe's $86.3B.

longterm.evidence: Management kept investing in Pro capabilities, supply chain and acquisitions through a three-year housing slump instead of cutting to protect near-term margins.

gr1.evidence: It is one of the largest US retailers, with $164.7B of FY2025 sales and a market value of about $295B.

ni10.evidence: Home Depot has reported net earnings every year for the last ten years, including $14.2B in FY2025.

gr4.evidence: Home Depot has paid a cash dividend every year since 1987 and raised its quarterly dividend to $2.33 in February 2026.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from about $5.46 in FY2015 to $14.23 in FY2025, far more than a one-third increase.

gr6.evidence: The share price is about 20.7 times trailing earnings, above Graham's 15x limit.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 20.7 times P/B of about 17.8 equals roughly 367, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Home Depot has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals; its edge is scale and execution.

timing.evidence: With 30-year mortgage rates at 7.28% on Oct 1, 2026 and existing-home sales depressed, the market timing for home improvement demand is unfavourable now.

th3.evidence: It is already the largest player in a huge mature market rather than a company that dominated a small niche first.

team.evidence: It has an experienced, long-tenured management team, but not a founder or world-class visionary, and CEO Decker is on temporary medical leave.

th5.evidence: Its 2,359 stores, website, Pro sales force and SRS's 1,250+ branches give it unmatched distribution to homeowners and contractors.

durable.evidence: Physical, bulky building materials and jobsite delivery are hard to disrupt online, so its position should largely hold over 10-20 years.

th7.evidence: Its Pro and distribution strategy is widely understood and copied by Lowe's and QXO, not a secret others miss.

trend.evidence: It is not a leading beneficiary of AI, cloud or another platform shift; its demand is driven by housing and repair cycles.

dr1.evidence: FY2026 EPS is guided to grow only flat to 4%, and forward EPS estimates rose just 2.3% from February to October 2026.

dr2.evidence: If mortgage rates ease and SRS/GMS integration lifts margins, results could look better in 18-24 months, but management sees no demand turnaround yet.

dr4.evidence: High mortgage rates (7.28% in Oct 2026) and weak housing turnover work against home improvement spending.

dr6.evidence: Potential catalysts include Fed rate cuts, a housing recovery, IEEPA tariff refunds and Q3 results around Nov 17, 2026.

dr7.evidence: With flat earnings guidance, a falling share price and CEO uncertainty, the case for a large concentrated position is weak.

gm.evidence: Gross margin is about 33.3% (FY2025), moderate for a retailer and not high enough to signal strong pricing power.

fcfyield.evidence: The free-cash-flow yield is about 5.1%, attractive for a market leader of this quality even with low growth.

gb2.evidence: FY2025 operating income of $20.9B is about 5.9% of an enterprise value near $356B, a modest earnings yield.

pa2.evidence: The slowdown stems from high mortgage rates and low housing turnover, a cyclical setback that should ease when rates fall.

pa4.evidence: The business is very unlikely to suffer permanent damage, but at about 19x forward earnings a further de-rating could still cause lasting price losses.

wo1.evidence: Home Depot is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Its product costs are not falling quickly with volume; gross margin has been flat around 33-34% for five years.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine multiple disruptive innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its ~$1.1 trillion market grows roughly with the economy and will not be many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Results are highly sensitive to interest rates, housing turnover and commodity prices such as lumber.

ns1.evidence: Scale lets it keep prices competitive and invest in service, but it has not systematically shared scale savings as Costco or Amazon do; gross margin has stayed flat.

ns4.evidence: Its Pro and SRS distribution build-out should strengthen its position over 10-20 years, but rivals Lowe's and QXO are pursuing the same strategy.

va2.evidence: It solves the large, recurring problem of getting the right materials and tools for home repairs and building projects quickly and reliably.

tn1.evidence: Home Depot is a traditional retailer serving the housing cycle, not a company built for a secular trend like AI, energy or robotics.

tn2.evidence: The market sees a DIY retailer, while it is becoming a large Pro and specialty-distribution company via SRS and GMS, but that change is widely recognised.

tn3.evidence: It is a large US company, not a commodity producer or startup, but its sales are seasonal (spring peak) and tied to the housing cycle.

tn4.evidence: It passes two of three: revenue grew in FY2024 and FY2025 and it is solidly profitable, though debt (about $52.9B) far exceeds cash ($2.1B).

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow has been positive every quarter, but cash ($2.1B at Aug 2, 2026) has been far below debt (about $52.9B) in every recent quarter.

tn6.evidence: Revenue grew 3.2% in FY2025 and is guided to grow 2.5%-4.5% in FY2026, well below 10%.

tn7.evidence: FY2025 revenue growth of 3.2% plus a free-cash-flow margin of 7.7% totals about 11, far below 40.

tn8.evidence: In FY2025 revenue rose 3.2% while SG&A plus depreciation rose about 6.9% (to $33,975M from $31,782M).

tn9.evidence: It hits several instant kills: debt far exceeds cash, operating margin is 12.7% (below 20%), and revenue growth is below 10%.

tn10.evidence: There is no major regulatory or legal threat; issues are routine (e.g., a 2021 EPA lead-paint consent decree and tariff policy).

tn11.evidence: It provides tools, building materials and services that help homeowners and contractors repair and improve homes, charging retail and distribution margins, chosen for its assortment, availability and Pro services.

tn13.evidence: Score about 50 of 130: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 5, short interest (1.2%) 10, institutional ownership (76%) 10, revenue vs expenses 0, 5-year return vs S&P 0, moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 5, secular trend 0, culture 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Over five years revenue fell in FY2023, operating margin dropped from 15.3% (FY2022) to 12.7% (FY2025), and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage (about 8.7x) and current ratio (1.08) pass, but assets excluding goodwill ($86.5B) are below liabilities ($92.8B) and liabilities are about 5.6x equity.

tn18.evidence: Decker has been CEO only since 2022, with margins and EPS down since then, and no open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: It beat EPS estimates in Q1 and Q2 FY2026 (adjusted $3.43 vs $3.41; $4.92 vs $4.71), but missed in Q3 FY2025 and operating cash flow missed consensus five quarters in a row.

tn21.evidence: No fraud or auditor issues, but operating margins have declined since FY2022 and it made two large acquisitions (SRS, GMS) in two years.

tn22.evidence: It has $164.7B of revenue, strong profits and cash flow, and does not issue shares to raise cash.

tn24.evidence: At about 19-20x earnings the price implies steady mid-single-digit growth plus margin recovery, above the ~1.6% three-year average revenue growth it has delivered.

tn25.evidence: Nash's DCF (1.6% growth, 9.9% FCF margin, 4% terminal growth, 12% discount, less $50.8B net debt) gives about $141 per share, below the $294 price.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E of about 19.2 is above Lowe's at about 15x, and the PEG of about 2.2 is well above 1.
